tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour who waters our plants is away this week.
The recipe which my aunt shared it needs less salt.
The library who opens on Sundays stays busy all day.
The bus that stops outside the school leaves at eight.
The park, that was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Who" correctly refers to a person in a restrictive clause that identifies which neighbour.

Tip: For people in defining clauses, "who" or "that" both work.

FALSE — Drop the leftover "it": the relative already fills the object slot — "which my aunt shared."

Tip: Never leave a second object pronoun after a relative that already stands for it.

FALSE — A library is a thing, so use "which" or "that," not "who."

Tip: Reserve "who" for people.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which bus; no commas needed.

Tip: No commas = the clause is essential to identify the noun.

FALSE — After commas (non-restrictive), use "which," not "that": "The park, which was closed…"

Tip: Commas signal extra information — and "that" is not welcome there.
tasks.solution_overview: Ask whether the clause names a person or a thing, and whether commas mark it as essential or extra. Then check that the relative itself carries the subject or object — no leftover "it."

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chef whose soup won the contest teaches on Saturdays.
The cyclist who's helmet cracked bought a new one.
The concert, which sold out in an hour, starts at seven.
The students that organised the bake sale raised enough for the trip.
The garage, who stores our bikes, needs a new lock.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Whose" correctly shows possession: the soup belongs to the chef.

Tip: If you can rephrase as "X's Y," you almost always want "whose."

FALSE — You need possession, not "who is": write "whose helmet."

Tip: "Who's" = who is / who has; "whose" = of whom / of which.

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" with commas correctly adds non-essential detail about the concert.

Tip: Extra information between commas takes "which" for things, never "that."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" for people is acceptable in defining clauses.

Tip: In defining clauses about people, "who" sounds slightly more formal than "that."

FALSE — A garage is not a person; use "which": "The garage, which stores…"

Tip: Places and buildings take "which," not "who."
tasks.solution_overview: Separate "who's" (contraction) from "whose" (belonging), and keep "who" for people while "which" covers places, buildings, and events.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival, that locals love, fills the square each July.
The tutor whom we hired last autumn still helps on Fridays.
The kettle which boils too slowly needs replacing.
The friend who we invited yesterday cannot come after all.
The photos that Maya printed them are still on the table.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A comma-bound clause must use "which," not "that": "The festival, which locals love…"

Tip: Spot the commas first; they ban "that" in careful exam English.

TRUE — Formal "whom" correctly marks the object of "hired."

Tip: If the relative would be "him/her/them," "whom" is the careful choice.

TRUE — Restrictive "which" correctly defines which kettle; no commas required.

Tip: British formal writing often prefers "which" even in defining clauses about things.

TRUE — Informal object "who" is widely accepted here; the sentence is grammatical as written.

Tip: Exams may prefer "whom" after a preposition, but bare object "who" is usually fine.

FALSE — Remove the residual "them": "The photos that Maya printed are still…"

Tip: The relative already equals the object; a second object pronoun is always wrong.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch non-restrictive "that," object relatives (who/whom), and pronoun leftovers. If the clause already does the object’s job, nothing else should sit in that slot.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The runner who finished first still looked fresh.
The map that we borrowed shows every hiking trail.
The café whose windows face the river stays open late.
The singer who's opening the show arrives at six.
The film which the class watched last week was subtitled.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Restrictive "who" correctly identifies the runner.

Tip: No commas when the clause is needed to pick out which person.

TRUE — Defining "that" correctly restricts which map.

Tip: "That" is a safe default in restrictive clauses about things.

TRUE — "Whose" can mark possession for things as well as people.

Tip: "The café whose windows…" = "the café’s windows."

TRUE — "Who's" correctly expands to "who is" before "opening."

Tip: Try expanding the contraction; if "who is" fits, "who's" is right.

TRUE — Restrictive "which" correctly defines the film.

Tip: Either "which" or "that" works in defining clauses about things.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound models: people with "who," things with "that/which," possession with "whose," and a genuine "who's" = who is. Use them as clean reference patterns.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The cousin with whom we share a flat cooks on Sundays.
The playlist, that includes every song from the trip, is private.
Anyone who's keys are missing should check lost property.
The museum which we visited last month displays local pottery.
The coach that designed the drills will explain them tonight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Preposition + "whom" is the formal, correct pattern for a person as object.

Tip: After a preposition, prefer "whom" (people) or "which" (things), not "who" or "that."

FALSE — Non-restrictive needs "which": "The playlist, which includes…"

Tip: Commas + "that" is a classic exam fail.

FALSE — Possession requires "whose": "Anyone whose keys are missing…"

Tip: If "who is keys" sounds nonsense, you wanted "whose."

TRUE — Defining "which" correctly identifies the museum.

Tip: Object relatives can keep "which/that" or drop the pronoun in informal style.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" for a person is acceptable in defining clauses.

Tip: "Who" is often preferred for people, but "that" is not an error here.
tasks.solution_overview: Preposition + whom is the polished form; commas still forbid "that"; and "who's" vs "whose" remains a high-frequency trap. Expand every contraction before you mark true.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery from which we order bread raised its prices slightly.
The volunteer whom neighbours praised organised the litter pick.
The novel that Sam finished last night it still sits on the shelf.
Brighton, which hosts the festival, fills with visitors in May.
The friends who cake the party brought later left early.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "From which" correctly links a thing after a preposition.

Tip: Keep the preposition with "which/whom" in formal answers.

TRUE — "Whom" correctly marks the volunteer as the object of "praised."

Tip: If you can replace the relative with "him/her," "whom" is justified.

FALSE — Delete residual "it": "The novel that Sam finished last night still sits…"

Tip: One clause, one object slot — never both relative and "it."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Brighton.

Tip: Place names with commas almost always take "which," not "that."

FALSE — Word order collapses; write "The friends who brought the party cake later left early."

Tip: Keep the relative clause’s internal word order like a normal statement after the relative.
tasks.solution_overview: Preposition + which, object whom, and residual pronouns dominate here. If a leftover "it" remains, cut it; if word order inside the clause collapses, rebuild it as a normal statement.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour to whom the parcel was delivered signed for it.
The suitcase who's zip is broken stays in the loft.
Drivers whose licences have expired must renew them online.
The beach that we walked along at dusk was almost empty.
The headteacher, that announced the trip, answered questions calmly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "To whom" is the formal object pattern after a preposition.

Tip: Preposition + whom is almost always safe for people in exam English.

FALSE — A suitcase’s zip needs "whose," not "who's."

Tip: "Who's" never marks possession — expand it and the error is obvious.

TRUE — "Whose" correctly marks possession for people in a defining clause.

Tip: "Whose" works with plural noun heads just as with singular.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which beach.

Tip: Object "that/which" can often be omitted: "The beach we walked along…"

FALSE — Non-restrictive about a person needs "who": "The headteacher, who announced…"

Tip: Commas + person → "who"; commas + thing → "which"; never "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "to whom," possession with "whose," and the ban on "that" after commas are the three checks here. Expand every "who's" before you mark the sentence true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The email which Jess sent yesterday still needs a reply.
The author of who the novel was written declined the interview.
The bridge that crosses the canal is closed for repairs.
Guests which arrive early may wait in the lobby.
The trainer whose tips improved my serve will join practice.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Defining "which" correctly identifies the email.

Tip: Subject or object relatives both allow "which/that" for things.

FALSE — After a preposition referring to a person, use "whom": "of whom the novel was written" (or better, rephrase).

Tip: "Of who" is almost never correct; "of whom" is the formal fix.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the bridge.

Tip: No commas when the clause picks out which bridge.

FALSE — Guests are people; use "who" or "that," not "which."

Tip: "Which" for people is a strong red flag in exam marking.

TRUE — "Whose tips" correctly shows possession.

Tip: "Whose + noun" is the clean possessive relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: People vs things and preposition + whom are the focus. Never use "which" for guests or classmates, and never leave "of who" after a preposition.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The notes, which the lecturer circulated, summarise the chapter.
The applicant whom the panel interviewed withdrew this morning.
Anyone who's still outside should come in before the rain.
The app that tracks sleep was updated overnight.
The room in which the rehearsal takes place is on the second floor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about known notes.

Tip: If removing the clause still leaves a clear noun, commas + "which" are right.

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly follows the panel as subject of "interviewed."

Tip: Swap in "him/her": if that fits, "whom" is justified.

TRUE — "Who's" = "who is" before "still outside."

Tip: Expand the contraction; if the sentence still works, keep "who's."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the app.

Tip: Everyday tech nouns follow the same who/which/that rules as any other thing.

TRUE — "In which" is the formal relative after a preposition for a place.

Tip: Formal writing prefers "in which" over a stranded preposition, though both can be grammatical.
tasks.solution_overview: These are clean mid-level models: non-restrictive "which," object "whom," a genuine "who's," defining "that," and formal "in which."

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The tent, that leaks in heavy rain, stays in the shed.
The clerk to who complaints should be sent sits at desk four.
Jars whose lids lack labels must be checked before use.
The witness who the lawyer called seemed unsure.
The recipe on which the cake depends needs soft butter.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "which" after commas: "The tent, which leaks in heavy rain…"

Tip: Everyday nouns follow the same comma rule as any other thing.

FALSE — After "to," use "whom": "to whom complaints should be sent."

Tip: Preposition + who is almost always wrong; make it "whom."

TRUE — "Whose" correctly marks possession for jars/lids.

Tip: "Whose" is fine for inanimate nouns in careful English.

TRUE — Object "who" is acceptable in modern usage for the person called.

Tip: Formal style may prefer "whom," but bare "who" as object is not marked wrong in most exams.

TRUE — "On which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Keep preposition + which together in formal answers.
tasks.solution_overview: Comma + "that," "to who," and possession for things are the main traps. Formal preposition + which/whom patterns earn easy true marks when you spot them.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The teammates with who we share a pitch signed the same form.
Edinburgh, which remains our favourite base, hosts the fringe each August.
The folder that Mia flagged contains old photos.
A classmate who's been seconded to the drama club still joins practice.
The prototype, which the lab tested last night, failed the heat check.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "whom" after "with": "with whom we share a pitch."

Tip: Any preposition before a person-relative wants "whom."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Edinburgh.

Tip: City names with commas take "which," not "that" or "who."

TRUE — Defining "that" correctly restricts which folder.

Tip: Ordinary nouns follow ordinary relative rules.

TRUE — "Who's been" = "who has been," a correct present-perfect relative.

Tip: "Who's" covers both "who is" and "who has."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds extra detail about the prototype.

Tip: If the noun is already identified, commas + "which" are the pair.
tasks.solution_overview: One clear "with who" error sits among solid non-restrictive and defining models. Confirm each true sentence’s person/thing choice and comma pattern before moving on.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide through whom we booked the tour confirmed the time.
Parcels that arrive damaged must be photographed immediately.
The gardener whose allotment we admired stays on until dusk.
The schedule for which we planned the weekend has changed.
Someone who's coat is still hanging here left early.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Through whom" correctly marks a person after a preposition.

Tip: Booking and arrangement phrases often need "through/with whom."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which parcels.

Tip: Everyday logistics nouns take the same defining "that/which" rules.

TRUE — "Whose allotment" correctly shows possession.

Tip: "Whose" works cleanly before a concrete noun.

TRUE — "For which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Prefer "for which" over informal stranded "which… for" in formal answers.

FALSE — Possession needs "whose": "Someone whose coat is still hanging…"

Tip: "Who's coat" expands to "who is coat" — never possession.
tasks.solution_overview: Four solid preposition and defining patterns frame one "who's + noun" trap. Expand the contraction and the false answer becomes obvious.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The dentist by whom the filling was done explained the aftercare.
Players which miss warm-up cannot start the match.
A rule whose wording is unclear should be rewritten.
The hall at which we rehearsed drew a large crowd.
Anyone who's locker number is faded should ask at reception.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "By whom" correctly marks the agent in a formal relative.

Tip: Passive-related "by whom" is formal but grammatical.

FALSE — People need "who/that": "Players who miss…"

Tip: Never use "which" for players, guests, or classmates.

TRUE — "Whose wording" correctly marks possession for a rule.

Tip: Documents and rules commonly take "whose" in exam English.

TRUE — "At which" correctly attaches the preposition to an event/place.

Tip: Prefer "at which / in which" in formal answers when asked.

FALSE — Use "whose": "Anyone whose locker number is faded…"

Tip: "Who's locker" = "who is locker," which never works.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "by whom" / "at which" sit beside people-"which" and "who's + noun" errors. Keep person/thing and contraction checks automatic at this level.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The friend in whom's flat we stayed later moved abroad.
Few of the tools on which the repair depends are in the box.
The baker that her sourdough won prizes has closed for a week.
Neighbours whom the council thanked stayed for photographs.
The shed where tools are kept, that flooded last spring, is locked.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Malformed possession; write "The friend in whose flat we stayed…"

Tip: Never stack "whom's"; use "whose" after the preposition.

TRUE — "On which" correctly links tools after a preposition.

Tip: "The X on which Y depends" is a high-value formal pattern.

FALSE — Replace "that her" with "whose": "The baker whose sourdough won prizes…"

Tip: "That + possessive" always signals a missing "whose."

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly refers to the neighbours thanked.

Tip: Subject of main clause + object relative "whom" is a clean formal structure.

FALSE — Mixing "where" with a second non-restrictive "that" is wrong; prefer "…, which flooded last spring,…"

Tip: A second relative after commas still cannot be "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Top-band items twist possession after prepositions and stack relatives. Reject "whom's" and "that her," keep "on which," and remember a second comma-bound clause still wants "which."

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The landlord to whose conditions we agreed released the keys.
Staff for whom flexitime was approved must log hours weekly.
The radio that the kids dismantled it cannot be put back together.
Lisbon, which we use as our summer base, hosts a street-food fair.
Anyone who's completed module three may sit the quiz.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "To whose conditions" correctly combines preposition and possession.

Tip: "To/with/under whose + noun" is advanced but correct.

TRUE — "For whom" correctly marks people after a preposition.

Tip: Approval/arrangement phrases often need "for whom."

FALSE — Remove "it": "The radio that the kids dismantled cannot be put back together."

Tip: Even in long sentences, residual objects are still errors.

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about Lisbon.

Tip: City names with commas take "which."

TRUE — "Who's completed" = "who has completed."

Tip: Present-perfect "who's" is possession’s innocent twin — expand to check.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "to whose" / "for whom" are trustworthy when the grammar fits; the leftover "it" is the only clear fail. Expand "who's" once more to confirm "who has."

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The mentor of whom we sought advice later joined another club.
A paragraph that its purpose is unclear should be cut.
Helpers who the organisers thanked now lead regional teams.
The portal via which parents upload forms went offline at noon.
The interim coach, that arrived in May, reorganised training.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Of whom" correctly marks the person after the preposition in a formal relative.

Tip: "Of whom we sought advice" is stiff but exam-correct.

FALSE — Use "whose": "A paragraph whose purpose is unclear…"

Tip: "That its" is the same broken pattern as "that her."

TRUE — Object "who" for people thanked is acceptable modern usage.

Tip: Formal alternatives use "whom"; both are usually accepted without a preceding preposition.

TRUE — "Via which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Tech/process nouns take "which" after prepositions, not "who."

FALSE — Non-restrictive about a person needs "who": "The interim coach, who arrived…"

Tip: Title + commas still bans "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "of whom" / "via which" contrast with "that its" and comma + "that" about a person. Diagnose possession failures and non-restrictive person clauses first.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The climbers with whom we shared a rope reached the ridge first.
Anyone whose rucksack holds food must hang it away from tents.
The rule under which the contest will be judged is printed on page two.
A volunteer who's already briefed the stewards need not attend the dry run.
The criteria against which entries are scored were agreed last autumn.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "With whom" correctly marks people after a preposition in a defining clause.

Tip: Shared-activity language often uses "with whom we shared…"

TRUE — "Whose rucksack" correctly shows possession.

Tip: Outdoor and everyday policies love "anyone whose + noun" constructions.

TRUE — "Under which" correctly links the governing framework.

Tip: Contest and club English frequently uses "under which."

TRUE — "Who's already briefed" = "who has already briefed."

Tip: Final check: expand "who's"; if "who has" fits, the sentence can stand.

TRUE — "Against which" correctly marks the standard of comparison.

Tip: "The X against which Y is scored" is a polished relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean advanced set: preposition + whom/which, possessive "whose," and "who's" = who has. Use these as your checklist for person, thing, possession, and contraction.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The shelf on whose edge the vase sat collapsed overnight.
Children for who the workshop was designed must be under twelve.
The camera that its battery died mid-shoot still needs charging.
The island off which we camped has no mobile signal.
Someone who's waiting by the gate should come inside now.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "On whose edge" correctly combines preposition and possession for a thing.

Tip: "On/in/at whose + noun" works for inanimate heads too.

FALSE — After "for," use "whom": "Children for whom the workshop was designed…"

Tip: Preposition + who is almost always wrong for people.

FALSE — Replace "that its" with "whose": "The camera whose battery died…"

Tip: "That its" is a possession failure in disguise.

TRUE — "Off which" correctly attaches the preposition to a place.

Tip: Geography often uses "off/near/beside which" in formal relatives.

TRUE — "Who's waiting" = "who is waiting."

Tip: Expand once; if "who is" fits, keep "who's."
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced possession after prepositions mixes with "for who" and "that its" traps. Fix person-preposition forms and replace broken "that + possessive" with "whose."

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The path along which we walked ends at the lighthouse.
A neighbour who's dog barks at dawn has apologised twice.
The committee members whom the mayor praised stayed for tea.
The oven, that overheats on the fan setting, needs a service.
Few of the routes by which hikers reach the summit stay open in winter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Along which" correctly links a place after a preposition.

Tip: Path/road/route phrases love "along/by which."

FALSE — Possession needs "whose": "A neighbour whose dog barks…"

Tip: "Who's dog" = "who is dog" — expand and reject.

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly refers to the members praised.

Tip: Subject of the relative clause + object "whom" is a clean formal structure.

FALSE — Non-restrictive needs "which": "The oven, which overheats…"

Tip: Commas still ban "that," even for household nouns.

TRUE — "By which" correctly marks the means/route.

Tip: "The X by which Y happens" is a polished relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal path relatives contrast with "who's + noun" and comma + "that." Expand contractions and check commas before you trust a late-set true.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The potter from whom we bought the bowls still runs Saturday classes.
Anyone whose laptop battery dies mid-flight should carry a spare charger.
The chapter after which the quiz begins covers relative pronouns.
A neighbour who's lived here since March already knows every shortcut.
The tune to which the choir rehearsed was written last winter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "From whom" correctly marks a person after a preposition.

Tip: Buying/learning phrases often use "from whom we bought/learned…"

TRUE — "Whose laptop battery" correctly shows possession.

Tip: Travel reminders love "anyone whose + noun."

TRUE — "After which" correctly links sequence for a thing.

Tip: Chapter/section English frequently uses "after which / before which."

TRUE — "Who's lived" = "who has lived."

Tip: Final check: expand "who's"; if "who has" fits, the sentence can stand.

TRUE — "To which" correctly attaches the preposition to a tune/thing.

Tip: Music and ceremony phrases often need "to which" in formal relatives.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean capstone of advanced but correct relatives: preposition + whom/which, possessive "whose," and "who's" = who has. Use these as your final checklist for person, thing, possession, and contraction.
